The history of computing hardware is often told as a story of miniaturisation, but a better frame is the story of moving data. Every generation of machine has been organised around a bottleneck, and the bottleneck has almost never been arithmetic. Early mainframes waited on magnetic drums. Minicomputers waited on core memory. Workstations waited on the bus between the processor and the graphics subsystem. In each era the designers who won were the ones who understood which wire was narrow and arranged the rest of the machine around it.

Modern accelerators have inherited the same problem in an exaggerated form. A contemporary chip can perform hundreds of trillions of floating point operations each second, but it can only read a few terabytes from its attached memory in that time. The ratio between those two numbers has been growing worse for two decades. A kernel that reads one byte for every operation it performs will sit idle almost all of the time, waiting for the memory system to deliver work. This is why so much of the craft of writing fast numerical code has migrated away from counting operations and towards counting bytes.

Language model inference makes the arithmetic unusually clear. When a model generates one token at a time, every parameter in the network must be read from memory exactly once in order to produce that single token. The amount of arithmetic performed on each parameter is tiny: one multiply and one add. So the time to produce a token is, to a first approximation, the size of the model divided by the memory bandwidth of the machine. A model of thirty billion parameters stored in one byte each, on a machine that can read three hundred gigabytes per second, cannot produce tokens faster than ten per second, no matter how fast its arithmetic units are.

Everything interesting in inference engineering follows from trying to escape that division. One escape is to make the numerator smaller by storing the parameters in fewer bits. Another is to make the denominator effectively larger by reading the parameters once and using them for several tokens at a time, which is what batching does for throughput and what speculative decoding does for a single stream. A third is to avoid reading some of the parameters at all, which is what sparse and mixture of expert architectures do by construction.
